confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- TEXT ---
Causation cannot be adequately analyzed as mere regular succession between types of events, for regularity accounts fail to distinguish genuine causal relations from accidental or common-cause correlations, since a falling barometer reading is regularly followed by a storm without causing it. Such accounts therefore leave open the possibility that any observed regularity might be spurious in precisely this way, offering no resources for isolating those patterns that reflect genuine production or influence rather than mere coincidence or shared antecedents. 
Interventionist accounts developed by Woodward succeed where regularity accounts fail by identifying causal relations with dependencies that remain invariant under ideal interventions on the putative cause. On this view a variable X counts as a cause of Y precisely when there exists a possible intervention on X that would change the value of Y while holding fixed all other relevant variables, thereby capturing a stable relationship that persists across a range of manipulations rather than one that merely happens to obtain in the actual course of events. 
The interventionist account explains the epistemic privilege of randomized controlled experiments, whose design approximates an ideal intervention by severing the putative cause from its ordinary antecedents. By assigning subjects to treatment or control conditions through a random mechanism, such trials break the usual connections between the intervention variable and its background causes, thereby isolating the dependence of the outcome on the treatment alone and furnishing evidence that would be unavailable from passive observation of regularities.
--- END ---
